name: Punch perm

card.summary: A tight, springy short men's perm from Japan that adds dense volume and texture to straight hair.
card.note: Strongly associated with yakuza and delinquent subcultures in Japan.

quick.overview:
The punch perm is a short, tightly curled men's hairstyle made with a chemical perm and thin irons. It gives straight hair a dense, curly, voluminous look.

It was invented in 1960s Kitakyushu, Japan, and was popular through the mid-1990s. Today it is a niche style, sometimes worn for its bold retro look.
quick.how: A barber applies perm chemicals to short-cropped hair and sets it on narrow hexagonal irons, producing tight curls that hold through washing. Results are said to last months.
quick.risks: Chemical perming can dry or damage hair. The style carries strong cultural associations in Japan, which affects how it is perceived.

lead: A punch perm (panchi pama) is a tightly curled short hairstyle for men, created with chemical perming and narrow irons.[1][2]
It was devised by barber Shigemi Naganuma of Kitakyushu, who reshaped his iron into a thin hexagonal form after round irons failed to grip hair tightly, and first called the style champion press.[1]

It was popular from the 1970s to the mid-1990s among yakuza, bosozoku bikers, truck drivers and construction workers, and declined as fashion changed.[1] For wearers it adds volume and a rugged texture to straight hair.

chain: Perm tight curls on short straight hair
angle.text: The perm gives straight hair tight, even curls and fullness, changing the silhouette of the head.

paras: The style features uniform tight curls over short hair, similar to an afro but made on straight hair, and is sometimes called the Japanese afro.[2] It resembles the jheri curl but with much tighter curls.[1]
Naganuma's hexagonal punch iron allowed rodless perming that held up to daily washing.[2] Barber Ryoichi Hijiya later helped spread the technique and received a Japanese honor in 2023.[2]
Its link to the yakuza and delinquent groups contributed to its decline. Few barbers are now trained in it, as more men use salons.[1] It appears in games and media as a retro reference.[2]

timeline.event: Naganuma creates the style in Kitakyushu.[1]
Hijiya receives a Japanese honor for barbering contributions.[2]
